newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's princess displeased with media reports.
newsitem.headline: Japan's princess displeased with media reports.

text.p: Japanese Crown Princess Masako criticised what she called "exaggerated" and "sensational" media accounts of her married life at a news conference marking her 33rd birthday on Monday.

In her first solo appearance at a news conference since she married Crown Prince Naruhito in June 1993, the diplomat turned princess took aim at both Japanese and foreign media coverage of her married life.

"Parts of these articles sometimes have content which may be thought-provoking," she said in response to a Japanese reporter's question about reports in an Italian newspaper and in the U.S. magazine Newsweek.

"However, viewed on the whole, they tend to emphasise overly specific aspects or themes, and in doing so, they sometimes cite examples which are not based on the truth or draw extreme conclusions," she said.
The Italian article carried the headline "Silently Suffering Princess".
As an example, Masako quoted the article as saying "she almost never appears in public."
"Is that really how it is? Is it not a bit exaggerated? It seems so to me," the princess said in a news conference held on Friday with Japanese reporters and released on Monday.
But video footage from the news conference showed the princess somewhat tentative in her answers and looking more drawn than when she married 3-1/2 years ago.

In the televised Despite Masako, daughter of Japan's U.N. ambassador Hisashi Owada, is a Harvard and Oxford graduate fluent in several languages who abandoned a promising diplomatic career to wed Naruhito.
At the time of her wedding, Japanese and foreign media speculated the cosmopolitan princess might breathe fresh air into the tradition-bound Imperial Palace.

However, Masako's rare public appearances and even rarer public speaking occasions gave rise to fears she was being pressured by courtiers trying to suppress her potential to open up Japan's secretive imperial household.
Earlier this year, Japanese media reports said Masako was suffering criticism from courtiers because she had not produced an imperial heir after 3-1/2 years of married life.

Masako lashed out at Japanese weekly magazines, which run a heavy diet of gossip, for feature articles she said were "based on preconceived notions, or which advance arguments centering on conjectures with no basis in fact".

Masako's criticism was the second time in a month members of her family have attacked the Japanese media, which generally treat the imperial family with a deference Britain's beleaguered royals would envy.
Last month, her brother-in-law Prince Akishino, held a news conference to deny magazine reports he was keeping a mistress in Thailand.
"The person who wrote the article must have very good imagination," said Akishino, Naruhito's younger brother.
"Smoke emerged from where there was no fire in the first place," said the prince, who is married with two daughters.
A Japanese daily newspaper welcomed the new approach to the press by the secretive Imperial Household Agency, the bureaucracy which oversees palace affairs.
"The Imperial Household Agency is beginning to view news conferences by members of the imperial family as a good way to convey their personal character to the public," the Asahi Shimbun said.
But Masako suggested she was unaccustomed to appearing in public on her own.
"At previous press conferences, His Imperial Highness was always at my side, so I felt secure knowing that I could consult with him if the need arose," Masako said.
"In that sense, I came here being a bit nervous today."
